hints: Look closely at which groups are attached directly to the central CH (the alpha carbon) in each amino acid, and which are out on the side chain.
Remember a peptide bond is always a condensation between the alpha-COOH of one amino acid and the alpha-NH2 of the other, not the extra groups in the R group.
walkthrough:
**Recall what makes a peptide bond**

A peptide bond always forms by condensation between a carboxylic group and an amino group.

One $-OH$ is lost from $-COOH$ and one $-H$ is lost from $-NH_2$, releasing water:
$$-COOH + H_2N- \rightarrow -CO-NH- + H_2O$$

**Spot the alpha groups and the side-chain groups**

Every amino acid has one central carbon (the alpha carbon) with one $-NH_2$ and one $-COOH$ attached directly to it. Any extra $-NH_2$ or $-COOH$ is part of the R group.

On the left amino acid, group 2 is attached directly to the CH, so it is the alpha amino group. Group 1 is on the side chain as part of an amide, so it is not alpha.

On the right amino acid, group 3 is attached directly to the CH, so it is the alpha carboxyl group. Group 4 is on the side chain, so it is not alpha.

**Choose the true peptide bond**

Protein synthesis only links the two alpha groups together, leaving the R groups free.

That means the bond must be between alpha amino group 2 and alpha carboxyl group 3.

options.A: Groups 1 and 4 are both side-chain groups, not the alpha groups, so they do not form the backbone peptide bond.
options.B: Groups 2 and 3 are the two alpha groups (alpha-NH2 and alpha-COOH), so condensation between them correctly forms the peptide bond.
options.C: Group 2 is correct as the alpha amino group, but group 4 is a side-chain carboxyl group and is not used for the peptide bond.
options.D: Group 3 is correct as the alpha carboxyl group, but group 1 is a side-chain amide group and is not used for the peptide bond.
